transcript.title: KENDRICK JARRELL BEAIRD, Petitioner, v. UNITED STATES, Respondent

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: We will hear argument this morning in Case Number 25 -5343, Beaird versus United States.  Mr. Page.

Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  For two reasons, the courts below erred in deferring to the commentary when interpreting Guideline 2K2.1.  First, the proper rule for deference to guideline commentary is no deference. Nothing in the text of the Sentencing Reform Act suggests that courts must ever defer to commentary when interpreting a guideline, let alone defer on the  -- according to the extreme rule of Stinson.  That alone should resolve the question presented given the baseline expectation that courts independently determine the meaning of legal provisions.  That expectation dates back  to Marbury, and it should be especially hard to displace in the criminal setting, where respect for liberty demands that we turn square corners.  In fact, the Sentencing Reform Act is affirmatively incompatible with any deference regime.  Section -- Section 3553(a)(4) requires that the Commission set forth the range of imprisonment in the guidelines, not elsewhere. And Sections 994 and 995 of Title 28 attach detailed procedural requirements to the  amendment of guidelines, which requirements do not apply to guideline commentary.  Why would Congress bother to require detailed notice, public comment, 180 days of congressional review, and the approval of four  voting commissioners every time the -- the Commission amends a guideline if the Commission  could simply bind the courts to a new interpretation of the guideline without going through all of this simply by amending the commentary?  The second reason the courts below erred in affording Stinson deference is that if the Sentencing Reform Act leaves room for deference, the proper predicate is genuine ambiguity of the kind that survives every tool of construction, not the mere absence of plain or flat inconsistency, as Stinson suggests.  The rule applied below, which requires courts to construe guidelines in ways that they  think are wrong, certainly can't be found in the SRA's text, and it is not consistent with the judicial role.  I am pleased to take the Court's questions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What do you do with Kisor?

The significant fact of Kisor is that it weakens the force of stare decisis in -- in -- because it -- it weakens Seminole Rock, and so, for that reason, the Court should return to first principles and reconsider the terms of the statute.  My first-line position, my primary rule that I suggest the Court ought to follow, is that it should simply review the text of the Sentencing Reform Act and ought to, therefore,  conclude that no deference is appropriate.  However, if it believes that  --that Kisor sets forth the appropriate rule for agencies, at least the rule here ought to be as favorable to judicial resolution of legal provisions as was Kisor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Of course, after Booker, the guidelines are advisory.  And  I'm not sure why we should invite the lower courts to engage in somewhat it strikes me as an academic exercise of interpreting.  Why don't they just look at what the Commission meant in the guidelines and move on to the 3553(a) factors?  I just think -- I'm not quite sure that, you know, Stinson is not a more workable regime.

The  --the simple answer is it is not the question -- it is not the process  that the Sentencing Reform Act calls for.  It is not what the statute calls for.  The statute indicates that the courts are to find the  sentencing range in the guidelines themselves.  It distinguishes between guidelines and commentary in terms of how they are created, and those are different categories of enactments, and, therefore, the guidelines must be determined independently.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: While they're different categories of enactments, I think what concerns me about your argument is that you're suggesting that they are separable in some way, which is really not the way in which the guidelines were devised.  And I think we sort of have a -- a fundamental misunderstanding of how the manual works because the guidelines and commentary are  actually inextricably linked.  And what I mean  by that is that sentencing judges use the Guidelines Manual to do what is essentially a calculation.  It's kind of like math, that the guidelines themselves have certain components  to them, and the commentary tells you how those pieces fit together, how you are supposed to take them into account.  When you are a judge, you're using both to reach the right answer under the guidelines, and there is a right  answer as to what the guideline range is.  And so what concerns me about your way of framing this is you suggest that the court can somehow look at the guidelines, not take into account the commentary, not defer to it, not use it, and yet still have an accurate guideline calculation, which is really not how the system is designed.  So can you  -- can you respond to that?

Of course.  Stinson presumes that the guidelines have a freestanding meaning.  Stinson says that the guidelines mean one thing, and if the Commission -- and if the commentary is plainly  inconsistent with them, we are to disregard them.  So the assumption that the Commission has always been using or should have always been using -- and it has -- is that you can determine a meaning from the guidelines alone and resort to the commentary  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But it's a very, very narrow category.  I mean, as Stinson understood it, the guidelines have a meaning, obviously, but if the commentary says something that is totally inconsistent, then you have a problem.  But, if it's not inconsistent, then I don't take Stinson to say you shouldn't be reading them in coordination, in conjunction.  The problem arises just when the judge doesn't know what to do because the guidelines say one thing and the commentary says something totally different.  What you're suggesting is that even when the two can be reconciled, the commentary can be disregarded and we don't have to pay attention to it in understanding the guidelines, and  -- and -- and that, I don't think, is how the guidelines are designed.

So it -- whether or not it is how the guidelines are designed, it is how the statute is designed.  The statute says that  the sentencing range is set forth in the guidelines.  The only mention of commentary in the Sentencing Reform Act is in 3553(b)(1),  which says that the commentary may be of use in determining when it is appropriate or not appropriate to depart.  So, if we look at the -- the text of the statute alone and we look at the cues from the structure of 994, specifically the heightened procedural requirements of guidelines in preference to commentary, we can tell a -- we can see a congressional intent that the sentencing range should be determined by  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I'm sorry.  Keep going.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well --
No, of course.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Stinson looked at all that 30 years ago and came to the conclusion that the commentary was binding,  controlling, force of law, and went through this whole exercise.  And since then, as the  Chief Justice said, the one major change in the sentencing realm is that those guidelines are no longer, as a whole, binding.  They're advisory.  So, I guess, Stinson plus Booker together suggests that we've already been down this road, it's been that way for 30 years. 1B1.7 of the  -- of the guidelines itself says the commentary has the force of law.  The commentary to that says that.  So, given all that, why are we reinventing the wheel when Stinson did this -- 30-some years ago?

Well, first of all, I don't think that we can say that -- that Congress or any other objective observer can -- could confidently say that Stinson sets forth the rule that governs the relationship between -- between commentary and guidelines at least since Kisor, right?  We  -- we -- we -- the -- the apple cart has already been upset, and now we are just trying to -- please.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Why?
I'm sorry?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Counsel  --
Yeah.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- why?  Why has Kisor upset the apple cart?
Well --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: We reference  --we reference Seminole Rock as an imprecise analogy, but we relied on the guideline, 1B1.7, which tells us that the commentary should  -- should be followed.  And we relied on Williams. And we relied on the structure of the guidelines system and said that  --and we announced the level of deference.  Why did Kisor upset that?
Well, first, we can answer the question empirically and see that in half of the circuits that under the --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, half the circuits may have gotten it wrong, but what does that have to do with anything?  The other half have said it has no application.  Other  than that uncertainty, the courts have been pretty clear of what to do, right?  Kisor's the only thing that introduced uncertainty.

Well, I mean, I think that's a bit post ergo, post hoc.  Since Kisor, there has been more uncertainty.  But, as Judge Bibas explained in Nasir, Kisor sort of  awakened us from a doctrinal slumber in which we  -- we moved from a position where, essentially, the -- the -- the commentary was  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Let me ask you how this operates, and  -- and let's take this note  --this -- this  --this guideline, okay? The  -- the guideline says the application -- let's look at the guideline.  It defines it as a semi-automatic firearm that is capable of accepting a large capacity magazine, okay?  That's the guideline.  That gives you the enhancement under the guideline. The application note says  -- makes it clear that this refers only to a firearm that  "at the time of the offense either had attached to it or had in close proximity a large capacity magazine."  If I read the guideline just as a guideline and it says you apply the enhancement to a semi-automatic firearm that is capable of accepting a large capacity magazine, I look at the structure of the gun, and if it's capable of it, I don't care where the magazine is or  what size the magazine is because the words of the guideline say capable.  So, if I decide that, wouldn't I be more punitive if I decided that "large capacity firearm" meant any firearm that was built to hold a large magazine?

In this particular case, no.  And the reason we take that position or the reason we believe that is that to say that  --that a gun is capable of accepting a large capacity magazine might mean that it is physically capable if a large capacity magazine  were present, or it might mean that --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But that's not what the guideline says.  All I'm suggesting to you is it's only by reading the application note do I know that the magazine has to be attached to it or have -- or be in close proximity.  It's only the application note that tells us.

My  -- respectfully, I disagree that that comes only from the application note, and the reason is that  capable  -- there is an ambiguity in what "capable of accepting a large capacity magazine" means.  It might mean capable --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But I'm  -- I'm a literalist.  Capable to me means you can do it.
What --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You can  -- you can give me any alternative you want, but if -- without the application note, you're creating a sea of confusion for district court judges to fill in the blanks --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- when the application note makes it very clear what it means.
So the application note does have some clarifying function, but  anything that the Commission could do to clarify in the text of a commentary it could do to  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So you're suggesting your rule is more workable than Stinson?
Yes, I do believe it is more  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  So now we have ambiguity as to what "capable" means. We have ambiguity as to how large the magazine has to be.  And that's less workable following the application note than your system of  letting every district court judge have to define these terms anew --
So  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- and decide what they mean anew.  That's more workable for you?

Well, so in  --a couple of things will assist in containing any  disuniformity in the precedent.  The first is that the courts can still use the  --the commentary as an interpretive aid, as they would under Skidmore, which will  --means that it will still have a sort of anchoring effect and contain any disruption to the system.  The second thing is that the  --the -- the  --the Sentencing Commission is uniquely created to respond to disruptions to its  precedent and to disuniformity in its precedent, and Congress's intended way of  dealing with disuniformity in the precedent is for them to meet every year and amend the text of the guidelines.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Do you think, Mr. --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's called -- sorry, please.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Do you think, Mr. Page, that the Commission needs to defer to the  Commission's policy statements, as Williams indicated?
The courts or the Commission?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I'm sorry, that the  -- that the  -- that the courts need to defer.
Interpretive policy statements I do not believe carry binding deference any more than commentary.  And that comes from, first of all, 3553(a)(4), which  says that the sentencing range is defined --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So that's  -- that's the opposite of what we said in Williams.  So you're asking us not only to overthrow Stinson but to overthrow Williams as well?

Well, no.  I think that in Williams, the Court was dealing with a -- was not dealing with an interpretive policy statement that amended another guideline.  It  was dealing with a policy statement that limited when we could depart  --when the court could depart from the guidelines, and that's all that was at issue in  --in Williams.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Not -- you don't take Williams to be talking about policy statements generally?

I don't take it to be talking about interpretive policy statements. I take it to be saying that policy statements can limit  -- and -- and this was the clear impact of 3553(b)(1) in the pre-Booker era -- when a court could depart and that they were effectively mandatory in that realm before Booker.  And there simply isn't  --there wasn't a guideline that the policy statement was interpreting.  So it's very difficult to see it as an interpretive policy concerning that.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Page, on stare decisis, it seems to me we -- we first have to acknowledge that the circuits are currently badly split and somebody is going to be -- existing law below is going to be rejected.
I  -- I think that's clear.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's yes.  And, second, we'd have to decide that interpretive principles are entitled to stare decisis  effect, something about which judges on this Court have -- have opined different ways.
Correct.  That's the second issue presented.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then the next thing we'd have to look at is the quality of reasoning.  And Stinson relied on silence being  enough to be an implicit delegation of -- of interpretive authority and that their ambiguity is the appropriate trigger, both of which we've since rejected in Loper Bright.
Indeed.  And it would have to require on silence to  --to create deference in the criminal setting particularly.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.  And you'd have to say that 994, which says, right, not even commentary but interpretive guidance is  -- plus 3553, which says to courts consider, is somehow an express delegation of interpretive authority, exclusive interpretive authority in  the Commission.
It seems, if that's a  --an express delegation, you will find express delegations of interpretive authority all over the place.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then you'd say  -- have to say, well, it's consistent somehow with Booker even though Booker -- the whole point of Booker is that everything's  supposed to be advisory in this area, not mandatory.
I think Your Honor is right.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then  -- and then, on terms of reliance, I mean, does any  criminal in the country rely on the commentary to the guidelines when deciding whether to commit a crime?
No.  I think the only reliance interests are those of the Commission, and they can be easily dealt with by moving text from  --to the commentary.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Can I just  --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  You -- you argue that Loper Bright undermined Stinson.  And Loper Bright concerned  executive agencies interpreting statutes instead of -- instead of courts interpreting them.  And I just don't see what Stinson, which involves an agency in the judicial branch and issues non-binding advice, really has much to do with Loper Bright at all.

Well, Loper Bright, first of all, it indicated that -- that statutes have a  -- a single best meaning rather than a range of permissible meanings, and it rejected the idea of an implied delegation of interpretive authority. Perhaps the Court could distinguish agencies and statutes on that ground and say that for some reason, those principles do not apply to regulations or agency -- agencies.  But, if it were to distinguish an agency, it oughtn't distinguish the Sentencing Commission, which deals with particularly the sentencing realm, where there is a  --ought to be a strong expectation that judges will resolve those  questions that determine the defendant's fate rather than defer to another actor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You began by saying the  --the rule in a case like this should be no deference.  Now the ultimate question here, as Justice Sotomayor was discussing, includes the term "large capacity magazine."  So let's  say you are a district judge and you are not to defer to the commentary of the Sentencing Commission as to what constitutes a large capacity magazine.  How do you go about deciding what that means?
You use the  --the text and the structure of the guidelines, just as you use the text and structure of the other --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, concretely. Concretely.  You have the term "large."  What is large?

"Large" means large for a semi-automatic firearm.  So whatever that is, it isn't 17, which is the average.  And we look at (a)(2), which provides -- excuse me, (a)(3), which provides the same adjustment for a large  capacity magazine that is provided for a bomb, a  -- or a machine gun or a sawed-off shotgun. And we ask, is the average gun really merit the same kind of adjustment?  Did the Commission mean that?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So the  --your -- your  --your methodology would be to examine all semi-automatic weapons and see what is the average, and so whatever is above the average, that would be the  -- the large capacity magazine?
So I don't know that  -- that something that's just above the median would necessarily qualify, and so there would -- there could be potentially edge cases. And  -- and -- and -- and  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But I just don't see how this could possibly work without some degree of deference to what is essentially a policy call by the Sentencing Commission.

The  --the Sentencing Commission is free to make that policy call.  It needs to do that in the text because that is where the stat -- the Sentencing Reform Act told them to resolve questions of that sort.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It has to be in a guideline?
It has to be in a guideline.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It can't be in a policy statement?

No.  In my view, it -- it cannot.  A policy statement is not  --does not have the binding authority to determine the guideline range.  And the reason that we know  that is because 3553(a)(4) says that the range is set forth in the guidelines and because -- because they are distinguished in 3553(b)(1) and because of the different procedure.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Do they go through notice and comment?
Typically, yes.  They don't have to.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Does commentary typically go through notice and comment?
Typically, yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What was your answer to the question whether we have to overrule Williams?  Yes or no?

I  -- the --the holding of Williams itself, no, I don't believe you do because the -- the -- Williams concerned a -- a  -- did not concern an interpretive policy statement of any kind, so we don't have to -- we also don't have a policy statement here.  We have commentary.  And those are distinguished  in 3553(b)(1) and throughout the Guideline Manual.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: One might wonder what practical difference the issue here makes. First of all, the guidelines are now simply advisory.  Second, the district court here  stated that "even if the guideline range was not calculated or applied correctly," it would have imposed the same sentence regardless of the applicable guideline range.
So  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So why does this matter for your client?

-- the Fifth Circuit has consistently  --well, not consistently, but it has often said that it does not take such  statements at face value, that it undertakes a separate harmless error analysis in that circumstance.  And that is a recognition of the fact that there are courts that say this in literally every sentencing case.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So it doesn't believe these judges?  You think  --he says -- they think these judges are lying when the judge says, look, I  --I've gone through this whole guidelines calculation, but it doesn't really  matter, I'd impose the same sentence even if the guidelines didn't come into play at all? That's a lie?

I don't know that it thinks that they are lying, but I think that it may think that they have included a boilerplate statement in  -- and that it may -- they may have over- --underestimated the impact of the guidelines on their own thinking.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Sotomayor?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I'm not sure I understood your answer to Justice Alito about Williams.  Williams said that policy statements  had to be followed, correct?  That's the same thing Stinson says, that commentary has to be followed.
It  --it said that in a particular context.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The context there was a policy statement that said that district courts couldn't do certain things, correct?
That it  --that they could not depart.  And that came from 3553(b)(1) because it had -- and it had an express statutory basis.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So a policy statement that operates the way this does, which talks about what something means, would have to  -- we would have to overrule that part of Williams's holding, correct?
I don't think that Williams expressly addressed that.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Williams said we had  -- district courts had to follow policy statements in all circumstances to calculate the guidelines.  That's how I read Williams's holding.
That question is not before you  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I know it's not, counsel.  Assume it were.  Would you overrule  that part of Williams?
Insofar as it affects this case, then that part of Williams --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I didn't say I took it out of this case.  If the holding in Williams, as I read it, was that district courts are required to apply the policy statements in calculating guidelines, would  that holding be overruled or more limited by your view under  --
If  --if the Court were of the opinion that that is the holding of Williams, it would be limited.  However, either --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What would be limited?
The holding of Williams would be limited to the  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That some part of  -- of Williams would have to be overruled, correct?
I  -- in my view, Williams does not speak to  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.
--the calculation of guidelines.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: We'll fight about that after.  We can go -- both go look back at it.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kagan?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So, again, on policy statements, Mr. Page, Congress specifically authorizes the Commission to issue policy statements.  Is that correct?
It does.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So we're not talking about implied or implicit delegations.  We're  talking about an express delegation to the Commission?

In my view, we are talking about an implied delegation because we are  talking about an implied delegation to create binding policy statements, whereas what -- what the  -- what is expressly delegated is the -- the ability to create policy statements of some kind.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  Well, we'll get to whether it's binding or not.  But there's an  express delegation authorizing the creation of policy statements, correct?  I mean, you have to say yes to that.
Obviously, yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And -- and -- and what a policy statement is is defined very broadly. The Commission can issue general policy statements -- and I'm -- I'm quoting here -- "regarding application of the guidelines or any other aspect of sentencing or sentencing implementation."  That's what the Commission can do, correct?
That is the statutory text, yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So  --so suppose that all the commentary in the sentencing manual was just relabeled as policy statements, that there's an express authorization to issue those, correct?
If  -- the Court -- the Sentencing Commission could redefine commentary  through the appropriate procedures as policy statement or as guideline if it wished to  change the legal effect of them.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, I mean, what I'm getting at is that the -- the policy statements have a very broad definition encompassing everything that's found in the commentary.  So,  if the Commission just took all the commentary and relabeled it as policy statements, Congress would have expressly authorized it.  I would think that the  --the result of that, the implication of that is that, of course, Congress meant for courts to follow it in the same way that courts have to follow -- you know, had to follow guidelines.

Well, so there are policy statements that Congress has specifically stated that courts must follow.  Those are in 3582(c)(1), (c)(2), 3583(d)(3), right?  There  is no general statement that courts must follow policy statements.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, there's not a general statement, but there's an express authorization to create these policy statements.  Do you think that -- that Congress meant that the Commission should create these  policy statements and then people could take them for whatever they were worth, that that's all it was?

Yes.  I mean, to the extent that a policy statement interprets a guideline, yes, that  --that is precisely what Congress intended if -- if it authorized interpretive  policy statements at all.  Now one reason that we know this is not a policy statement is, number one, they are expressly distinguished from commentary in 3553(b)(1), and, second, because the Commission has consistently distinguished between policy statements and commentary.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Gorsuch?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: 994 says they may issue policy statements silent as to commentary.
Correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So, first, we'd have to somehow conflate those two.
Correct, and in spite of 3553(b)(1).

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then 3553(a) generally says, you consider the commentary and the guidelines -- sorry, the --the guidelines and the policy statements.
Correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If we found that were enough to commit to the Commission the power to issue binding, on courts, binding interpretations, what would be left of Loper Bright?
Well, I mean --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Because doesn't every agency have the power to issue  -- most agencies have the power to issue interpretive rules --
I think you would have to find that there is a  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- and guidance documents?  That's all within their power. And  -- and, here, all Congress has said is consider them.
Correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It would be a pretty --
I will  -- I will say that  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- pretty big hole in Loper Bright.

Well, I  --I will say that I don't  -- I'm not sure that the -- the force of the precedent at issue here would necessarily -- necessarily has to extend beyond the sentencing context.  There is -- well, it's even under --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Oh, you don't  -- you don't think -- you don't think the federal  government's other agencies would come in here and say, we've got similar language?
I think they would say it.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.
Right.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then  --and then doesn't Congress know how to tell us when it wants us to follow policy statements?
It  --it does.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I'm looking at 3553(e), for example, just one example, that in those circumstances, the sentence shall be imposed in accordance with the guidelines and policy statements.  There it is.
Correct, correct, in several places throughout the code.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Several places.  So, if  -- if -- if we're looking at contextual clues, we would say this is very different than those?
Indeed.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  And then Williams, I thought that to be about 3553(b), which is no longer enforceable.
Correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.  Thanks.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kavanaugh?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: On Justice Kagan's question about policy statements versus the commentary, I'd be interested in what you do with 994(a)(2), where it says policy statements are regarding application of the guidelines and  the commentary is typically labeled application notes.  The same word, "application," would suggest that that commentary is a policy statement because policy statements are regarding application of the guidelines.  Just  curious on your thoughts on that.

Well, so two points about that.  The first is that I think, when it refers to a general policy statement concerning application of the guideline, it's talking  about things like 1B1.10, 1B1.13, or 6A3, the standard of proof, that address questions about how to apply the guidelines without determining -- that -- that -- but they're not talking about the category of offender or the category of offense.  Those are to be determined by the guidelines, and we know that from 3553(a)(4).  Now, whether the -- the Commission intended to say that policy statements -- that commentary was a policy statement because it used the term "application notes," to me, that doesn't quite follow because they also labeled it commentary, and the statute itself indicates in 3553(b)(1) that those are specific.  They also attach commentary to policy statements, which would be strange -- a strange thing to do  if they were the same.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Then, on Congress's understanding, I guess, of  --of the process, 1B1.7, as I mentioned earlier, since 1987 has specifically said commentary is to be construed to have the same force as policy statements.  What do you do with that?
So  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Congress has never -- even though Congress has actually, as  you know, overturned certain commentary, Congress has never reacted to 1B1.7 or the commentary to 1B1.7, which has been in place since 1987 on this.
Congress does not legislate by acquiescence.  It does not legislate merely because  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But it gets the guideline amendments each year, and the House and Senate Judiciary Committees get that, and I think its understanding would -- everyone's  understanding since 1987 was -- confirmed by Williams and Stinson, was that those policies  -- those commentary is -- has the force of policy statements.
Well, so I  -- I --I do not agree that the Commission giving Congress  notice that it wants to  --to promulgate a species of enactment  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's a fair point.  That's a -- that's a fair point.  On -- on -- just quickly on Williams and Stinson, I mean, Williams -- Stinson says  the principle that the Guidelines Manual is binding on federal courts applies as well to policy statements, and Williams, we said, where a policy statement prohibits a district court from taking a specified action, the statement is an authoritative guide to the meaning of the applicable guideline.  And then the next page, 43, of Stinson says, our holding in Williams dealing with policy statements applies with equal force to the commentary before us here.  I mean, I think you have a little bit of a problem with Williams if you're -- you're fighting pretty hard on that.

Well, the -- the -- the strange  -- I mean, that language in Williams is a little bit strange for its context.  It's talk  --it says the meaning of the guidelines, but it's not really talking about the meaning  of any individual provision.  I think what it meant to say, what it was saying when it said "the meaning of the guidelines" is the outcome dictated by the Guidelines Manual.  And it was speaking about  that in the context -- in a very different sentencing system, where the Guidelines Manual dictated a particular result, and it wasn't talking about a provision that -- that changes the meaning of a guideline.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Last one.  Justice Gorsuch's good questions about Loper Bright and what's binding.  I mean, isn't Booker a game-changer on that in the sense that whatever you come up with as a district judge in terms of following the guidelines, following the policy statements, following the commentary, is then only advisory and the district judge then can determine whether to vary up or down.  And it seems to me that really distinguishes this from kind of the whole executive branch situation at least potentially.  I want to get your reaction to that possibility that Booker mitigates the concern there.

So Booker doesn't change the fact that the -- that the Sentencing Reform Act commits a piece of legal text, requires a court to  -- and -- and requires a court to interpret it.  And the baseline expectation is that when that occurs, that legal issue will be decided by an Article III judge.  It's no different, say, than a Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure which said --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Then it's not going to be binding at all, the judge, I mean on anyone, right?
Well, I mean, it's binding on  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Given Booker?
It's not binding as to the ultimate sentence.  It still has determinate legal consequences.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.
It states what  -- what courts must do to explain the sentence.  It affects the standard.  It is reviewed de novo  by a court, and a defendant can -- and a court can be reversed for failing  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.
--to get it right.  Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Barrett?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So the Sentencing Reform Act tells district courts that they have  to follow the guidelines, putting aside Booker here, but, you know, they do have to, and we've  said to district courts that you have to accurately calculate the guidelines range even though you can depart from it.  What if the Sentencing Commission adopted a guideline saying that the commentary authoritarily  --authoritatively interprets our guidelines?
So  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Stronger than 1 -- 1B17 because that's a little bit equivocal.  It may give background.  It could be reversible error.  So, if -- if that guideline were amended to say something very definitive, what would your response be?

If the Commission did that through notice and comment, it called that new guideline a guideline, it would be within its power to do, it would be strange because there  is a lot of things in the commentary that do not directly interpret a guideline, so it wouldn't be clear how to make binding force of it.  But -- but, if Your Honor's point is that the  -- the -- that the Commission can interpret its own guidelines through a guideline, of course, it can.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It just seems then that this is all about nomenclature.
Right.  So it is a label chosen by the Sentencing Commission, and that label has a consequence of -- according to the Sentencing Reform Act.  So  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, why is it so important to you if, as a practical matter, the commentary goes through the same process as the guidelines do, goes through notice and comment,  Justice Alito asked you about this, and then goes to Congress, just like the guidelines.  Then what is the practical difference?

So the  -- the practical -- I mean, the difference -- the important difference is that these are different  categories of enactments that are set forth in the Sentencing Reform Act.  We could treat all commentary as binding if it goes through notice and comment, and perhaps that would be -- achieve Congress's goals maybe, but that's not the way that Congress chose to  --to -- to create its goals. And the  -- to achieve its goals.  What it chose to do was to create three different categories of enactments and that the -- and that only guidelines would determine the sentencing range.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Why do you think the Commission -- is it your sense that the  Commission, by calling this commentary, is somehow pulling a fast one, getting things into the commentary that it might not be able to put into the guideline itself?

So the Commission has been staffed by conscientious public servants who are conscientious of their role, and they have not attempted in general to -- to -- to circumvent anything.  But the  -- the -- the more important point is that this speaks to congressional  intent.  It speaks to congressional intent that  it would not have undermined the procedural requirements that it stated in 994 by permitting the -- the Sentencing Commission to do that or even leaving that opportunity on the table.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  One last question about Stinson and stare decisis.  I'm thinking about probation offices.  You know,  they're the ones that calculate in the PSR, and, presumably, the commentary application notes are very helpful to probation officers.  So is the idea that if Stinson goes, probation officers are then interpreting the guidelines and can't treat the -- you know, de novo themselves and can't treat the application notes as  --you know, or give deference to the application notes?

So, I mean, the application notes will still be available as -- as an interpretive aid.  It's not that anybody has to  cover their eyes when they are interpreting a guideline.  But I would say that anybody who is trying to reach a correct result about the  meaning of the guideline must confine themselves to the guideline when determining  what is dispositive in deciding the meaning of that.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Jackson?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So I guess I was a bit confused in your response to Justice  Kavanaugh that Congress doesn't operate by acquiescence in this area.  That is not the case.  I mean, isn't the entire way the sentencing system is structured that the Commission forms its guidelines, commentary, policy statements, or whatever, and it submits it, the whole package, omnibus, to Congress, who then, if they don't do anything, it becomes the binding "law," pre -Booker law, that we're talking about?  So it -- it seems odd that we would even be thinking that there might be a situation in which the Commission is smuggling in something in commentary because that's really not the way this works.

So I -- I certainly agree that the Commission has not attempted to smuggle anything in and that -- and that in practice it -- it hasn't behaved that way.  Now Congress does -- a congressional acquiescence, because it has delegated the power to write guidelines, does mean that guidelines become effective merely because Congress doesn't act.  But Congress  -- congressional acquiescence doesn't change the structure of the Sentencing Reform Act.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, I understand, but you're -- you're  --you're sort of dancing on the head of a pin, I think, because Congress gave the Commission this authority from the beginning, and the Commission structured the system in the way that it is.  Congress mentioned these things in the legislation but gave the Commission the ability to set up the scheme.  And the Commission decided, we're going to call this part guidelines, we're going to save the commentaries to help you apply those guidelines, and then we'll have these policy statements.  So I  -- I just worry about your taking so much stock in these different categories.  Let me -- let me ask you a more general question, which is the entire system, when we're talking about congressional intent, I thought, was set up to cabin judicial discretion with respect to sentencing, and so it's actually, at its very baseline, different than the world of administrative discretion and  the kinds of things that Justice Gorsuch talked to you about, right?  In this world, we have a background principle of judges not having discretion because that's the whole point of the guidelines system.  So it's a little troubling that you're now suggesting that the deference determinations and limitations that exist outside of this world should be imported in this way.
Well, they were imported by Seminole Rock, right, and so the --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Not into the guidelines.  They were started by Seminole Rock.  They were imported by Stinson, right?
Correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But Stinson was pre-Booker in a world in which the guidelines were sort of operating as a mandatory legal system.  And this goes back to the Chief Justice's point.  Now the guidelines are a recommendation to judges.  And so to suggest that there should be judicial deference in calculating the guidelines, it -- it sort of up-ends the whole system.  I don't know how it works anymore if  --
So  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- if we have that.

--in -- Booker changed the ultimate legal force of a guideline to the point -- to the extent that a -- a defendant no longer -- I mean a court no longer has to sentence within a range barring certain circumstances.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I understand, but the point of the guideline was to establish a baseline.  Similarly situated defendants were going to be treated similarly under the guidelines system because the Congress said we don't want, you know, judges exercising their  discretion in this way.  And so, if that's the whole point, it seems odd to inject into the guidelines system the baseline judicial discretion.  And that's  what you're asking us to do by looking at the deference doctrines in the exterior, in the other part of agency world, and importing them into this world.

In my view, there's a difference between judicial discretion to sentence within a range under (a)(2), to  interpret (a)(2) under the -- the particular -- apply (a)(2) to the particular facts of a defendant, and the  -- the --the task of interpreting a guideline in order to determine the  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And why do you think that judges have that discretion?  That's my point.  Why do you think that judges  -- Congress intended for judges to have the discretion to interpret the guidelines  inconsistently when they are calculating them?
My view is that they do not have the discretion to -- to interpret them inconsistently.  They  --they are commanded --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: To interpret them individually without  --
-- to interpret them correctly.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- without the Commission's input.  And, as Justice Alito  said, that means every judge just goes, what do I think large is, in looking at this guideline, leading to inconsistent calculations.  And I  guess I'm wondering why you think Congress would have wanted that in this context.

Congress had a particular mechanism in mind to contain differing opinions of the guidelines, and that is 994(o), and that is to have yearly amendment cycles in which they are expressly commanded to review the input from different stakeholders and the decisions of the -- the courts in order to  determine whether there is disuniformity and then to resolve that through 994(o).  This Court recognized that in Braxton.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.
Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  Mr. Feigin.

Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Our position is really the only one that's faithful to this Court's precedents. Stinson interpreted the Sentencing Reform Act to incorporate the same measure of deference for guidelines commentary that Seminole Rock gives to an agency's interpretation of its own rules.  Kisor then clarified what Seminole Rock deference means.  Add those two decisions  together and you get that Kisor applies to guidelines commentary. That said, I don't want to overstate the difference between our position and the position of the amicus here.  I  --we believe that even under Kisor, the guidelines are going to continue to be informed and interpreted in most instances by the commentary where there is commentary.  Our difference is simply the very small area where the commentary may take an interpretation that is an unreasonable  interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or even tries to override unambiguous guidelines text.  But we wouldn't think that happens very often.  On the other hand, Petitioner wants to swing the pendulum way in the other direction  and have a regime of no deference under which individual district judges are just free to interpret for themselves the advice that the Commission is trying to give them, notwithstanding what the Commission is telling them.  That would be a massive upheaval that would probably cause some kind of revision to  the guidelines that, of course, wouldn't solve all the retroactive problems with the cases that are still in the system.  And there's no  point.  It makes all the sense in the world, when the Commission is reasonably saying what the Commission is trying to say, to listen to the Commission.  And that's exactly where our Goldilocks position here lands.  Now I've kind of taken Petitioner's counsel to have essentially conceded the  point -- I'm sorry, Justice Thomas.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Feigin, there's been some discussion that Booker changed the landscape.  Would you elaborate on that a bit from your perspective?
Okay.  And I think I need to make two elaborations because I'm kind of in the middle here with two different directions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.

As to whether it affects Stinson, I don't think it affects the idea that  Seminole Rock deference is the appropriate measure of deference for guidelines commentary because, if anything, deferring makes even all  the more sense when it's simply advisory and not binding the way we envision normal agency rules under Kisor to be.  As between our position and the amicus's position, we also don't think that it makes a difference in the sense that I don't think that it would mean that the commentary,  which we acknowledge is a different species of promulgation from an actual -- actual guideline text or  -- or even a policy statement, we don't think that it would affect the amount of  deference the commentary should receive.  And it shouldn't mean that commentary could override an unambiguous guideline or adopt an unreasonable interpretation of an ambiguous one.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Feigin, you accuse amicus of trying to reconceptualize Stinson and the entire legal practical framework that underlies it through this express delegation theory that he's positing now and that no circuit has ever adopted, despite the fact we have a 6-6 split and pretty much every judge in America has written on this.  You stand by that, right?
We do not think that the commentary as it's been promulgated by the Commission can either be viewed right now as a  policy statement or as a guideline.  That's correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Nor do you argue that the statutes before us command express delegation to binding views from the  -- from the Commission.  I mean, you rejected that. You  -- you say that Stinson is premised on Seminole Rock, which is a theory of implicit delegation through silence, not explicit delegation through 994, for example.
I wouldn't quite say that, Justice Gorsuch.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I -- I don't see it anywhere in your brief, that argument.

So, Your Honor, first of all, Stinson itself looks to both 3553(b) and 1B1.7.  Beyond that, though, Your Honor, we have, I think, express post-Stinson action from Congress that acknowledges commentary and the force it can have.  Number one, you have the PROTECT Act and  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, I -- I understand  -- I understand you wind up in a similar place.  But the way you get there is entirely different.  Amicus says that 994 and  3553 evince an express delegation for the Commission to write binding  -- binding authority.  You say no.  Stinson -- Stinson is  an Auer case, a Seminole Rock case, and it's through silence and  -- and ambiguity that deference is required.  Totally  --totally different rules.
Your Honor, I don't think it's quite silence and ambiguity.  Our main difference with the amicus is whether  commentary actually is a policy statement.  I -- I will acknowledge it's --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, I know -- I know you agree with that as well -- disagree with that as well, but it does seem to me -- like, let's take the government's arguments on its own terms.  What do we do with the fact that the idea that silence as delegation has been rejected by Loper Bright and we said that ambiguity is a trigger that we -- we just don't even know how to apply, it's not a meaning we  --it's a fiction, the Court said.

Well, Your Honor, I think the particular situation that we have here is  different.  First of all, as I was just saying, I think at least as we look at it today, even if you think Stinson was incorrect in the first instance to interpret the Sentencing Reform Act  to adopt the measure of deference from Seminole Rock and  -- or --or  --or simply even in thinking commentary is a thing the Commission can do, we have 40 years of practice and then Congress in 2002 in the PROTECT Act itself modifying commentary to make sure that it's consistent with the guidelines in the  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I get that's a stare decisis argument.  But I was asking you, you know, just as an original matter, how can you defend silence as  --as --as a delegation and ambiguity as a trigger, and I haven't heard an answer to that yet.

Your Honor, so I think one thing that the Commission is certainly  entitled to do under (a)(1) is to promulgate a guideline.  They promulgated  --one of the guidelines they promulgated is 1B1.7, which expressly references commentary and the role that it can play.  And I took Petitioner's counsel just now to effectively concede that the Commission can issue a guideline that, when it wants it congressionally reviewed, would give some weight to commentary.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Sure.  It absolutely could.
Now, Justice Barrett, I think 1B1.7 has more  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It absolutely could.
Sorry.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Feigin, it absolutely could.  No one -- no one questions that, I don't think, before us.  And Congress provided a way for it to do it.  But isn't it a topsy-turvy world where commentary is binding but the guidelines aren't post-Booker?
Well  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And let me  --let me just spin it out a little bit further.  And why bother?  I mean, Petitioner acknowledged that as a practice, the Commission does put its -- much of its commentary through notice and comment.  But it doesn't have to.  It doesn't  even have to give it to Congress.  What kind of incentives structure would we create by saying:  Hey, you can put  binding things over here, that you don't have to do any of the protective things the guidelines are associated with, and then just put the cherry on top?  No one thinks that the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, the advisory notes are  binding, even though they rest on statutory authority not dissimilar to 994.

So, Your Honor, I think the binding nature goes to different things. The commentary is binding with respect to the interpretation of the guidelines, where at least it's not unreasonable and the guideline text isn't -- isn't unambiguous.  And then the guidelines, the question of whether they're binding is whether they're binding on federal sentencing courts in the ranges of sentencings that they can set.  You could see that the guidelines themselves might  not be binding on sentencing courts in that context, and that's what the Court held in Booker.  But that doesn't say that you couldn't have commentary that's binding on the interpretation of the guidelines themselves while they remain advisory.  And I think that's  exactly the regime that we've always had for 40 years.  The guidelines --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And isn't it important?  Isn't it important?  Because, if  you don't have that, it's hard to understand how the guidelines actually operate as a starting point or a baseline or anything in the world that we have.  In other words, I thought the whole point was to try to reduce unwarranted sentencing disparities by having the Commission issue some kind of document that tells judges  what it believes the sentencing range should be as a result of these facts that exist in a particular case.  If each fact and each factor can be separately decided by a judge, it's very hard to see how you're going to get a consistent baseline in order to have a sentencing system. One of the things I'm worried about is the statistics and the data collection function  of the Commission because, right now, the Commission uses the offense level as a proxy  for understanding the seriousness of an offense, and it runs all these calculations based on the offense level, assuming we have a consistent determination of offense level across similarly situated defendants.  If the system changes in the way that Petitioner suggests and each judge can determine the factor on their own, you won't have the same ability to determine what's happening in the system.  Do you understand what I mean by this?

Yes, Your Honor.  I think that's absolutely right.  And I think, as you  were pointing out during Petitioner's portion of the argument, the guidelines and the commentary have, since their inception, been designed as kind of interlinked with one another.  And Congress has recognized that interlinked structure when it amends common -- guidelines directly, it sometimes -- it amends the commentary.  It did that in the PROTECT Act in 2002.  And then we have a couple examples in our brief, the Artists Rights Act and the Stop  Infringement Act, in which Congress directly amends inter- --sorry, doesn't directly amend, but it directly instructs the Commission to  consider changes to commentary that we would consider directly interpretive commentary.  One of the pieces of commentary it directed the Commission to reconsider was the definition of the term "uploading."  The other was the definition of the term "infringement amount."  I don't know how much more direct Congress can get in making clear that this is a kind of thing that the Commission is empowered to do, and it's a kind of thing that would have  at least some effect, or there's very little point in Congress instructing the Commission to reconsider the --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Your argument there is  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. -- Mr. Feigin, what  --what would be the practical consequences of overruling Stinson?  I'm told that there were 66,000 defendants sentenced in federal courts, federal district courts, in 2025.  Do you have an estimate of how many of those sentences relied on commentary and would have to be done over?

I don't, Your Honor, but if you look at, for example, just 2K2.1, it's essentially impossible to apply it in the first instance without -- in many cases, without referencing the commentary, which will tell  you, for example, that the definition of "crime of violence" is to be found in 4B1.2(a).  It -- it -- the guidelines often use commentary to explain cross-references.  They give explanatory examples.  One piece of commentary that I think would be really central and subject to upheaval and very difficult for  the Commission to do as an actual guideline text would be in 1B1.3, which is the relevant  conduct guideline, which is central to defining the conduct that the judge is supposed to consider when applying the guidelines.  If you look at, for example, Notes 3 and 4, they're about jointly undertaken activity, and that's defined as the -- the conduct that a defendant's accountable for is  defined in the text as conduct that's in the scope of the joint activity, that's in furtherance of it, and that it was reasonably foreseeable.  But  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Is it reasonably  --is it reasonably foreseeable that overruling Stinson would require the resentencing of,  what, 10,000 defendants from 2025 alone?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah?  Especially since, apparently, district courts, according to some courts of appeals, can't be believed when they say I would have done the same thing even if the guidelines had not indicated this?

So, Your Honor, I think we'd argue that in a lot of those cases, the courts reached the correct result notwithstanding having referenced the commentary.  But I think that I  --I have no reason to disagree with that estimate insofar as it would --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, Mr. Feigin, you  --you didn't  --
-- be the number of sentencing claims we might face.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- you didn't make a floodgates, the -end-of-the -world argument anywhere in your briefs.  And we all agree that  after Edwards versus Vannoy, there's no habeas review for constitutional rules of criminal procedure.  I don't know why there would be here.  And on --
Well  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- and on direct review, as Justice Alito pointed out, district courts often do the belts-and-suspenders approach, saying I do this one way or the other.  We have harmless error review.  We have  the opportunity, as Justice Barrett said, to -- to have a guideline saying commentary.  We have (o), which is the actually prescribed statutory means.  Just amend it every year as you're supposed to.  And  -- and the government will benefit sometimes too.  I mean, there are some commentary that the government opposes because it thinks it's too lenient.  So it's going to work both ways.
Well  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What do you say to that?

-- Your Honor, everything you pointed out is an ameliorative measure.  But, if you have 66,000 sentencings a year, under Peugh, they all have to apply the old guidelines that were in effect at the time the  defendant committed his offense.  And because of Peugh, any changes that aren't in a defendant's favor can't be retroactive to those particular defendants.  So, for all of those cases, courts are still going to be at sea.  And there are going to be years and years and years of those cases  because, of course, the statute of limitations is five years, and it sometimes takes cases longer to get to trial.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Feigin?
As for the -- yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Sorry.  I'm sorry.
No, Justice Kagan, please.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If  --if Kisor applies to commentary, does Kisor also apply to policy statements?

I think that would be a very interesting question, Your Honor, on which we haven't taken a position here, but I think there is an argument that Kisor would apply there at least insofar as we think it affects the commentary in that I  --I think a legitimate question would arise whether even policy statements can override unambiguous  guideline text or do something that would be unreasonable  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean  --
-- in light of ambiguous text.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- I -- I read Stinson.  The first block of Stinson really  says we just want to follow the Williams rule. You know, this is the same as Williams.  It's  only later on in the opinion that the Court brings in the Seminole Rock analogy and says this is kind of like the -- the --the interpretation of agency regulations.  But it  -- it does suggest that, like, there needs to be the same rule, right?
